items.title: Why you should believe the hype for the EXTREMELY LARGE TELESCOPE (visiting ESO HQ!)
items.summary: AD | Get started with Brilliant’s tutor for free at https://brilliant.org/drbecky and save 20% off an annual subscription | I’ve come to the European Southern Observatory Headquarters to find out why…
items.body:
AD | Get started with Brilliant’s tutor for free at https://brilliant.org/drbecky and save 20% off an annual subscription | I’ve come to the European Southern Observatory Headquarters to find out why you should believe the hype for the Extremely Large Telescope. I’ll be chatting to some of the scientists who are going to use the ELT for their scientific research; using the biggest telescope to solve some of astrophysics biggest problems! From finding Earth-like planets orbiting other stars, to studying growing supermassive black holes, and resolving distant galaxies.

Previous videos:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NI8gwNwHwf0
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ss3CPR59gtI
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yjwB85IEcBY

00:00 - Introduction
02:07 - Exoplanets
08:28 - Stars orbiting black holes
11:15 - Galaxies
18:51 - The Distant Universe
00:00 - Bloopers

Video filmed on a Sony ⍺7 IV
Video edited by Martino Gasparrini: martino.freelance@gmail.com
Video produced by Marina Hui & Dr Becky Smethurst

---

👩🏽‍💻 I'm Dr. Becky Smethurst, an astrophysicist at the University of Oxford. I love making videos about science with an unnatural level of enthusiasm. I like to focus on how we know things, not just what we know. And especially, the things we still don't know. If you've ever wondered about something in space and couldn't find an answer online - you can ask me! My day job is to do research into how supermassive black holes can affect the galaxies that they live in. In particular, I look at whether the energy output from the disk of material orbiting around a growing supermassive black hole can stop a galaxy from forming stars.

items.title: What Is a No Space Vacuum?
items.summary: A normal vacuum is space without particles. But some quantum-gravity models begin with something stranger: no ordinary space at all. In Group Field Theory, the Fock vacuum contains no quanta of geomet…
items.body:
A normal vacuum is space without particles. But some quantum-gravity models begin with something stranger: no ordinary space at all. In Group Field Theory, the Fock vacuum contains no quanta of geometry. In certain models, large collections of these quanta could give rise to familiar space.
It's a theoretical possibility, not an observed origin story.

items.title: The Best Telescope For Beginners (My Top 4!)
items.summary: These are my top 4 options for getting started in astronomy and astrophotography. COMPLETE GUIDE: https://astrobackyard.com/buying-your-first-telescope/ Buying your first telescope is exciting, but ch…
items.body:
These are my top 4 options for getting started in astronomy and astrophotography.

COMPLETE GUIDE:
https://astrobackyard.com/buying-your-first-telescope/

Buying your first telescope is exciting, but choosing the right one can be confusing. In this video, I compare four different ways to explore the night sky, including a Dobsonian, a smart telescope, a compact astrophotography refractor, and a computerized telescope.

THE 4 OPTIONS:

1. 8-INCH DOB: https://bit.ly/3XmBefN

For the classic experience of looking through an eyepiece and seeing the Moon, planets, and bright deep-sky objects with your own eyes.

2. SMART TELESCOPE: https://bit.ly/3Ym1hoH

For beginners who want an easy, app-controlled way to capture and share images of the night sky.

3. DEEP-SKY IMAGING: https://bit.ly/3M6fiAK

For anyone ready to build a dedicated imaging setup and photograph colorful nebulae and galaxies. You’ll need a separate camera, tracking mount, and supporting equipment.

4. GOTO OBSERVING: https://link.amazon/B06N28K7F

For impressive views of the Moon and planets, with computerized object finding and tracking. I also discuss its potential for planetary imaging and the limitations for deep-sky photography.

I’ll walk through portability, ease of use, the “wow factor” through an eyepiece, and photography performance to help you choose a telescope you’ll actually enjoy using.

Some links above are affiliate links. If you purchase through them, I may earn a commission at no additional cost to you. Thank you for supporting AstroBackyard!

#Telescope #Astronomy #Astrophotography

items.title: Viral satellite image with CRAZY pattern explained #shorts
items.summary: Did you see this bunching of satellite trails on this incredible viral picture? Looks weird, but has a completely everyday explanation. So this was a picture by astrophotographer Brendan Larsen, who t…
items.body:
Did you see this bunching of satellite trails on this incredible viral picture? Looks weird, but has a completely everyday explanation.

So this was a picture by astrophotographer Brendan Larsen, who took 578 images each with an exposure of 8 seconds of the same view over a 2 hour period. And then he layered them all on top of each other to reveal just how many satellites there are orbiting the Earth right now, and why this is such a huge problem for professional astronomy, and anyone who wants to enjoy a dark night sky.

But what stood out to me in this picture is this clumping of satellite trails all together. They start out fairly well spaced but then closer together until they all appear to disappear over the same spot on the horizon.

These are the Starlink satellites, launched by SpaceX to provide internet wherever you are in the world. There’s just over 11,000 up there at the minute, but SpaceX’s plan is to eventually have 4 times as many.

And those satellites operate together in a grid, or constellation, so that they all go overhead at roughly the same angle in a given time period, as the Earth rotates underneath.

So that’s why there’s so many that pass directly overhead on roughly the same path, but then as they get closer to the horizon look like they’re all disappearing in the same place.
Think of train tracks, those nearby you can see are two parallel tracks, but if you look into the distance because of perspective those two tracks look like they’re getting closer together.

The same is happening here, directly above your head a satellite is only around 500km away, but as it gets towards the horizon it’s more like 2500km away.

You don’t get this bunching for the other satellite trails in the image because they’re all on different orbits. But there’s still a lot of them, in just 2 hours.

This is why this is such a big issue for professional observatories that stare at a faint galaxy for hours at a time to collect enough light. If a satellite blazes overhead it can ruin that observation, and waste in demand scientific resources. It’s a big deal for the likes of the Extremely Large Telescope that’s currently being built in Chile - at 39m across it’s the largest and most sensitive telescope ever built. To find out more about the ELT and the engineering that makes this whole project possible check out my latest video, and follow along for more about not just what we know in space, but how we know it.

Video filmed on a Sony ⍺7 IV
Video edited by Martino Gasparrini: martino.freelance@gmail.com

items.body:
The Planck length is roughly 1.6 × 10⁻³⁵ meters. People often call it the smallest possible distance, but nobody has demonstrated that. It marks a scale where our present theories of gravity and quantum physics may need replacing. That isn't proof that space comes in pixels.
Companion to Is Spacetime Made of Something?
